what_its_for: Fluvoxamine is used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), which involves unwanted repeated thoughts or actions that are hard to control. It may also be used for social anxiety disorder and other conditions as directed by your doctor. It belongs to a group of medicines called SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), which help balance certain chemicals in the brain to improve mood and reduce anxiety.
how_to_take: Take fluvoxamine exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with a meal or snack. Swallow the extended-release capsule (Luvox CR) whole — do not crush, chew, or break it open. Take your dose at the same time each day to help you remember. Do not suddenly stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, as stopping too quickly can cause dizziness, nausea, or other uncomfortable symptoms.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over time to find the right amount for you. For regular tablets, adults typically start at 50 mg once daily at bedtime. The dose may be increased every 4 to 7 days. Most adults take between 100 mg and 300 mg per day. If your daily dose is more than 100 mg, your doctor may have you split it into two doses — a larger one at bedtime and a smaller one in the morning. For extended-release capsules (Luvox CR), adults usually start at 100 mg once daily at bedtime. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store fluvoxamine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children. Do not use medicine past its expiration date. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking fluvoxamine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Do not take fluvoxamine if you are taking MAO inhibitors (such as phenelzine, tranylcypromine, or linezolid) — this combination can cause a serious, life-threatening reaction. Wait at least 14 days after stopping an MAO inhibitor before starting fluvoxamine. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it may cause drowsiness or dizziness. Avoid smoking, as it may reduce how well this medicine works. Tell all of your doctors and your pharmacist about every medicine, vitamin, and supplement you take, because fluvoxamine can interact with many other drugs including blood thinners, certain pain medicines, and other psychiatric medications.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience: thoughts of hurting yourself or suicide, especially in the first few weeks of treatment or after a dose change; sudden changes in mood, behavior, or unusual excitement; signs of serotonin syndrome such as agitation, confusion, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle twitching, or loss of coordination; severe skin rash, hives, or difficulty breathing (signs of an allergic reaction); unusual bleeding or bruising; seizures; or eye pain, redness, or vision changes. Contact your doctor if you notice increased anxiety, restlessness, or trouble sleeping when starting the medicine, as these effects are usually temporary but should be monitored.
when_it_works: Fluvoxamine does not work right away. Most people begin to notice some improvement in sleep, appetite, or energy within the first 1 to 2 weeks. However, it may take 4 to 6 weeks or sometimes up to 12 weeks of regular use before you feel the full benefit for OCD symptoms. It is important to keep taking it even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without speaking to your doctor.
special_populations: Children and teenagers: Fluvoxamine is approved for children aged 8 and older for OCD. Young people may be more likely to have thoughts of self-harm when starting antidepressants. Parents and caregivers should watch children closely, especially in the first few weeks. Older adults: Older adults may need a lower dose and should be watched more carefully for side effects such as dizziness and falls. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. There are risks and benefits to consider, and your doctor will help you make the safest choice for you and your baby. Liver problems: If you have liver disease, your doctor may start you on a lower dose and increase it more slowly.
